title: A Machine-Learned Comorbidity Index
claim: A shared scalar score learned by aligning score similarity with multiple outcome-label similarities captures outcome-specific nonlinear risk.
layout: Three-part, left-to-right flow with loss feedback loop and right-side outcome panel
description: A wide diagram with three regions. On the left, a rounded box shows diagnosis codes for an admission passing through a DeepSets-style permutation-invariant encoder to produce a scalar severity score s_i. At the top center, a rainbow bar runs from None to Mild, Moderate and Severe. It orders admissions by score, with person icons at both ends and a red-highlighted high-severity group. The center dashed box has three linked parts. On the left is a binary outcome-label similarity matrix built with a delta kernel. In the middle is the nHSIC formula with kernel definitions and a max-weighted-objective box. On the right is an RBF-kernel score similarity heatmap in yellow, green and blue. A dashed loss arrow returns to the encoder. At the far right, two small plots show nonlinear severity-response curves for Outcome 1 and Outcome T.
caption: MLCI: learning a shared severity score via multi-outcome nHSIC (centered kernel alignment).
abstract: Traditional comorbidity scores (e.g., Charlson and Elixhauser) are widely used for risk adjustment and patient stratification, but they have two key limitations: (i) they are largely mortality-centric and do not align well with other clinical outcomes, and (ii) their linear, rule-based structure cannot capture nonlinear, outcome-specific risk relationships. We propose a Machine-Learned Comorbidity Index (MLCI) that maps diagnosis codes to a single scalar by maximizing the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (nHSIC) between the learned score and multiple clinical outcomes. MLCI captures nonlinear risk-outcome dependence and is supported by a theory that characterizes when a unified, informative admission-level ordering can be achieved across outcomes. Empirical results on multiple benchmark electronic health record (EHR) datasets show that MLCI outperforms strong baselines across multiple evaluation metrics.
